prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
On the evening of April 13, 1970, some 200,000 miles from Earth, the crew of Apollo 13 was finishing a routine television broadcast. Commander Jim Lovell, command module pilot Jack Swigert and lunar module pilot Fred Haise had been in space for about fifty-five hours, and they were on course for the Fra Mauro highlands of the Moon, where they planned to be the third crew to walk on its surface. The mission had launched two days earlier, on April 11, with a minor glitch when one engine of the Saturn V's second stage shut down early, but the other engines had burned longer to compensate. Swigert had joined the crew only days before liftoff, replacing Ken Mattingly, who had been exposed to German measles. After the broadcast, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the cryogenic tanks in the service module, a routine task that mixed the super-cold oxygen and hydrogen so that the gauges would read accurately.

When Swigert flipped the switch for the oxygen tank fans at about 9:07 in the evening, Houston time, there was a bang, and the spacecraft shuddered. Lovell, looking at his instruments, saw a warning about low voltage on one of the main electrical buses, and a moment later Swigert spoke the words that became famous in a slightly altered form: "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Over the next several minutes the situation worsened. Two of the three fuel cells, which produced the ship's electricity and drinking water, were dying, and the pressure in oxygen tank number two read zero. Then Lovell glanced out a window and saw a stream of gas venting into space, which told him that the service module was losing its oxygen supply entirely.

The cause was later traced to a chain of small errors that began years earlier. Oxygen tank number two had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory, damaging an internal tube. During ground testing before launch, the tank would not drain properly, and technicians used the heaters to boil off the oxygen, running them far longer than the tank's thermostats had been designed to tolerate, because those switches had never been upgraded to handle the higher voltage used at the launch site. The overheating burned the Teflon insulation on the wires inside the tank. When Swigert turned on the fans, a spark ignited the damaged insulation, pressure rose rapidly, and the tank ruptured, blowing off a panel of the service module and crippling the neighboring tank as well.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and his team of controllers recognized quickly that the Moon landing was out of the question and that the goal had become survival. The command module, Odyssey, would soon run out of power and oxygen, so the crew was told to move into the lunar module, Aquarius, which was designed to support two men for about two days on the lunar surface. It now had to keep three men alive for four. Before they left, Lovell and Swigert powered down the command module carefully, because its batteries would be needed for the final return to Earth, and the whole procedure had to be improvised under time pressure.

The next decision was how to get home. Because Apollo 13 was on a free-return trajectory, it would swing around the Moon and be flung back toward Earth even with no further engine burns, but the path would have missed the intended landing area in the Pacific, and the trip would take too long for the consumables on board. Engineers decided to use the lunar module's descent engine, which had been built for landing, to speed the spacecraft's return. The first burn, made about five hours after the explosion, put the ship on a faster path. After the crew looped around the far side of the Moon, setting a record for the greatest distance humans had ever traveled from Earth, a second, longer burn shortened the trip further, bringing splashdown to Friday, April 17.

The hardest problems were the quiet ones. To save electricity, the crew switched off almost everything in Aquarius, including the heaters, and the cabin temperature dropped to near freezing, with condensation beading on the walls. Water was strictly rationed, with each man drinking only a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a kidney infection that worsened with dehydration. Sleep was nearly impossible in the cold, and the astronauts were tired, hungry and increasingly irritable. Meanwhile, carbon dioxide was building up in the cabin. The lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which absorb the gas, were designed for two men over two days, and as the levels climbed toward the danger zone, the crew had spare canisters from the command module, but they were square and the lunar module's receptacles were round.

Engineers on the ground gathered the same items that the astronauts had on board, such as plastic bags, cardboard from flight manuals, suit hoses and duct tape, and worked out a way to join the square canister to the round opening. They read the instructions to the crew step by step, and the result, an awkward device the crew called "the mailbox," pulled the carbon dioxide level back down. Another crisis came when it became clear that the navigation platform in the lunar module could not be aligned in the usual way, because the damaged service module had left a cloud of debris around the ship that confused the star sightings. Lovell used the Earth's terminator, the line between day and night, and then the Sun, to line up the ship for a midcourse correction, and he held the attitude by hand for a burn that had to be accurate to a small fraction of a degree.

Mattingly, the astronaut who had been grounded, worked in a simulator in Houston to figure out how to restart the command module from its dormant state using as little power as possible. His team developed a new procedure, tested it, and passed it up to the crew, who had to restart a spacecraft that had never been powered up from such a cold condition in flight. As the ship approached Earth, the crew jettisoned the damaged service module, and for the first time saw the extent of the damage, a whole side panel missing and wiring hanging out. They then moved back into Odyssey, released Aquarius, which had saved their lives, and prepared for entry.

On April 17, Odyssey met the atmosphere. The heat of entry caused the usual communications blackout, which was expected to last about three minutes, but it stretched past that, and the silence in Mission Control grew heavy. Then, at about four minutes and twenty seconds, Swigert's voice came through, and the controllers erupted. The command module's three parachutes opened above the South Pacific, and Odyssey splashed down near the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima at about 12:07 in the afternoon, Houston time, after almost six days in space.

Apollo 13 never landed on the Moon, but it is often called a successful failure, because the crew's survival depended on the ingenuity of people in space and on the ground. A review board led by Edgar Cortright identified the faulty tank and its heater system as the cause, and NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks, removed the dangerous wiring, and added a third tank, separate from the others. Apollo 14 flew the following January, and the program went on to land on the Moon four more times.
